lesson.title: Lipids: Defined Not by Structure but by an Aversion to Water
lesson.summary: Lipids are a chemically diverse group of biomolecules united by one property, their nonpolarity, and that hydrophobic character explains why they store more energy than carbohydrates and why they alone can form the barriers that separate every cell from its surroundings.
lesson.body:
Every biomolecule class covered so far is defined mainly by a shared chemical structure. Lipids break that pattern. Triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids look almost nothing alike structurally, yet biochemists group them together because they share one defining property instead of one defining shape: lipids are hydrophobic, or at least strongly nonpolar in the bulk of their structure, which makes them insoluble in water but readily soluble in nonpolar solvents like oil. That property traces back to functional groups, or rather their scarcity. Where carbohydrates are covered in polar hydroxyl groups that attract water, most of a lipid's structure consists of long hydrocarbon chains, carbon and hydrogen linked by nonpolar covalent bonds with no charge separation to interest a water molecule.

Most lipids still follow the biological logic of building larger molecules from smaller components through condensation reactions, even though lipids as a class are not true polymers built from one repeating monomer the way starch is built purely from glucose. A triglyceride, for example, forms when a three carbon alcohol called glycerol reacts with three separate fatty acid molecules, each condensation reaction linking a fatty acid's carboxyl group to one of glycerol's hydroxyl groups, releasing a water molecule and forming an ester bond each time. Digesting a lipid runs that chemistry backward: lipase enzymes hydrolyze those ester bonds, adding water back across each linkage to release free fatty acids and glycerol that intestinal cells can absorb.

Biologically, lipids do jobs that carbohydrates and proteins cannot do as well, largely because of that hydrophobicity. Energy storage is one: fats pack roughly twice as much usable energy per gram as carbohydrates, about nine kilocalories per gram compared to roughly four, because fat's carbon atoms are almost entirely bonded to hydrogen and to each other rather than to oxygen, so there is more chemical potential energy left to extract when those bonds are eventually broken during cellular respiration. Insulation and cushioning is another: fat under the skin and around organs resists heat loss and absorbs mechanical shock. Structure is a third, and arguably the most essential: phospholipids self assemble into the bilayer membranes that enclose every cell, a feat only possible because part of the molecule repels water while another part embraces it.

Lipids also carry out signaling functions carbohydrates rarely do. Steroid hormones, all built from a shared four ring backbone, travel through the bloodstream and, because they are lipid soluble, slip directly across the phospholipid membranes of target cells to bind receptors inside, rather than needing a surface receptor the way many water soluble hormones do. Vitamins A, D, E, and K are lipid soluble as well, meaning they travel through the body and store in fatty tissue rather than dissolving in blood plasma the way water soluble vitamins do.

The sections that follow break lipids down by structure: fatty acids, the hydrocarbon chains that make up triglycerides and phospholipids; the saturated versus unsaturated distinction that determines whether a fat is solid or liquid at room temperature; triglycerides, the body's primary stored fuel; phospholipids, the membrane builders; and sterols, the ring shaped lipids typified by cholesterol. Each is a variation on the same theme, a molecule built to avoid water, put to a different biological use.
